title: Health effects of sleep deprivation
markdown:
## In plain English
Research shows that not getting enough sleep harms many aspects of health and performance: it worsens cognitive functions (attention, memory, decision-making), increases pain sensitivity, impairs endurance exercise performance, and alters eating/weight-related behaviors. Regular factors that modify these harms (like exercise and caffeine) can influence outcomes: caffeine near bedtime reduces sleep quantity and deep sleep, while physical activity can both protect against some effects of sleep loss and improve sleep quality in older adults.

## Key findings
- Caffeine consumed too close to bedtime reduces total sleep time (~45 minutes), lowers sleep efficiency (≈7%), delays sleep onset (~9 minutes), increases awakenings after sleep onset (~12 minutes), reduces deep sleep, and increases light sleep; guidance from pooled data suggested avoiding coffee about 8.8 hours before bedtime (different caffeinated products had different recommended cutoffs) [PMID 36870101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36870101/).
- Experimental sleep deprivation lowers pain threshold and tolerance in healthy people and increases spontaneous pain intensity after partial sleep loss; evidence about worsening pain in people with chronic pain is limited and uncertain [PMID 36334461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36334461/).
- Acute or chronic sleep loss impairs cognitive performance including attention, memory, alertness, judgment, and decision-making, according to narrative reviews summarizing experimental and observational work (mechanisms are not fully understood) [PMID 37045455](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37045455/).
- Sleep deprivation produces a moderate negative effect on endurance exercise performance (meta-analysis of 31 studies, n = 478), with larger decrements for longer (>30 min) exercise bouts; study quality varied and many trials had unclear risk of bias [PMID 36472094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36472094/).
- In rodents, regular moderate exercise reduced cognitive and anxiety-like consequences of experimentally induced sleep deprivation, suggesting exercise may protect against some negative effects through multiple molecular pathways (preclinical evidence) [PMID 37898446](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37898446/).
- In middle-aged and older adults, randomized trials synthesized in a network meta-analysis found aerobic exercise was most effective at improving overall sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), whereas yoga ranked best for some specific components (sleep duration, efficiency, daytime function) [PMID 38450497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38450497/).
- Short or poor sleep is associated with increased energy intake, snacking on high-fat/high-carb foods, and changes in metabolic hormones that can hinder weight loss and weight maintenance (review of intervention and observational studies) [PMID 35458110](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35458110/).
- Among athletes, reviews report clear negative effects of sleep deprivation on reaction time, accuracy, strength, endurance, and cognitive functions relevant to performance; conversely, sleep extension can improve several performance measures [PMID 31288293](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31288293/).

## How strong is the evidence?
The body of evidence includes several meta-analyses and systematic reviews (higher-level evidence) for specific outcomes: caffeine effects on sleep [PMID 36870101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36870101/), sleep deprivation effects on pain [PMID 36334461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36334461/), endurance performance [PMID 36472094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36472094/), exercise interventions for sleep in older adults (network meta-analysis of 28 RCTs, 3,460 participants) [PMID 38450497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38450497/), and preclinical meta-analysis of exercise protecting against sleep-deprivation harms in rodents [PMID 37898446](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37898446/). Other summaries are narrative reviews (lower level) synthesizing experimental and observational data on cognition, athletic recovery, and weight regulation [PMID 37045455; PMID 31288293; PMID 35458110]. Sample sizes and study quality vary widely across topics (e.g., endurance meta-analysis pooled 31 studies, n=478; the network meta-analysis pooled 28 RCTs, n=3,460). Results are generally consistent that sleep loss harms cognition, pain sensitivity, endurance, and weight-related behaviors, but the strength of causal inference differs by outcome and study design.

## Limitations and caveats
- These abstracts do not cover every health outcome linked to sleep deprivation (e.g., long-term cardiometabolic disease, immune function) so conclusions are limited to the reported topics.
- Several findings come from animal studies or experimental sleep-deprivation models (rodent work; experimental human sleep deprivation), which may not fully generalize to chronic, real-world sleep loss in humans [PMID 37898446; PMID 36334461].
- Some evidence is from narrative reviews or trials with variable quality and risk of bias; for outcomes without randomized pooled data, causal claims are weaker [PMID 37045455; PMID 31288293; PMID 35458110].
- The caffeine meta-analysis gives quantitative cutoffs based on included studies, but applicability depends on the caffeine dose/formulation used in each study and individual differences in metabolism and sensitivity [PMID 36870101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36870101/).

## Sources
Based on 8 PubMed abstracts: 4 meta-analyses, 3 narrative reviews, 1 systematic review. Abstracts only, not full papers. Includes pooled evidence (a meta-analysis or systematic review).
